The Five Trust Signals Every B2B Website Needs

PublishedAugust 10, 2026
Last updatedAugust 10, 2026
AuthorFionn LennonFounder, Legency Media
Share
On this page
Section

Your B2B website gets judged by people who will never speak to you first. Gartner’s research on the B2B buying journey puts the share of purchase time buyers spend meeting potential suppliers at 17%. A typical buying group runs to six or ten decision makers (Gartner, The B2B Buying Journey).

Split 17% across three shortlisted vendors and any single sales team gets around 5% of the buyer’s attention. The B2B website carries the rest.

That is why proof beats polish. This piece sets out the five signals buyers look for, where each belongs, and what we measured ourselves. Where we quote a number, we say where it came from.

What makes a B2B website look credible?

Credibility comes from four things, and design is only the first. Nielsen Norman Group’s research names them as design quality, upfront disclosure, comprehensive and current content, and connection to the rest of the web (Aurora Harley, NN/g, 8 May 2016).

Most B2B websites are strong on the first and thin on the other three. The design is clean, the pricing is hidden, the last blog post is fourteen months old, and nothing links out to anywhere.

There is a commercial signal in the search data too. Advertisers pay $23.86 a click for “b2b web design agency”, $23.16 for “b2b web design” and $23.87 for “saas web design agency” (Semrush, us database, August 2026). Companies bidding at that level are buying attention. What the page does with the attention decides whether the spend earns anything.

Which client logos actually prove a B2B website is credible?

Recognisable names beat volume, and named permission beats both. A wall of twenty unfamiliar logos reads as filler. Four logos a buyer recognises reads as a reference list.

Two rules make a logo strip work. Use companies your buyer’s peers would name. Get written permission before you publish.

Teams skip the permission part, and it is the part that bites. Our own ask is short. Tell the client you are updating the website. Ask whether they are happy for their logo to appear in a client section. Say plainly that nothing elaborate is involved.

A logo-only request clears far more often than a full case study request, because it costs the client nothing to approve.

Keep a record of who said yes and when. A logo strip you cannot evidence is a legal problem waiting for a quiet week.

What makes a number on a B2B website believable?

A number is believable when a buyer can imagine the source. “18 months average client relationship” survives a follow-up question because invoices exist. “300% growth” does not, because nobody says growth in what, from what, over what period.

Three tests before a number goes on the page. Name the unit, name the window, and be ready to show the source if asked.

We hold ourselves to this, and it costs us claims. Marketing blogs circulate trust-badge and testimonial statistics freely: a 15% to 25% conversion lift from a compliance badge, a 270% lift from stacking five trust signals.

We traced the popular ones back and found no disclosed method, no sample size and no control group behind them. They do not appear in our client documents and they will not appear here.

The reverse case matters too. On one Irish manufacturer’s homepage we sampled in June 2026, a genuine “150,000 customers” claim sat in plain text. The site carried no review or rating markup anywhere. The claim was true, and a machine reading the page had no way to treat it as more than a slogan.

Where should security badges sit on a B2B website?

Next to the action they de-risk, not in the footer. A compliance badge answers a question the buyer is asking at the moment they commit, so it belongs beside the form or the button.

For B2B software, the badges that carry weight are the ones a security reviewer will ask about anyway: SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR handling, and where data is hosted.

One caution on placement. Badges near a form compete with the form for attention. They work best small, greyscale and directly under the submit button rather than beside the first field.

We have never run a controlled test on badge placement on a client site, so we will not tell you the size of the lift. A badge no reviewer can find does nothing at all.

How specific does a B2B website testimonial need to be?

Specific enough that it could only have been said by that person about you. A named person describing a concrete before-and-after beats three anonymous quotes about professionalism.

The strongest testimonial format we use follows a simple shape. What the situation was. What changed. What that meant in the buyer’s own units.

“We went from waiting five days for a website update to getting them the same day” carries more than “great to work with”, and a reader can check it.

Ask for it properly. We request a fifteen to twenty minute conversation about the client’s experience and offer a small credit as a thank you. We then send the written quote back for approval before anything goes live. Written approval is what lets the quote stay up.

How do you improve B2B website conversion rates?

Test the words on the button before you redesign the page. The largest single conversion change we have measured on a client site came from changing call to action copy rather than layout.

The test ran for 21 days between 6 and 27 March 2026 on a B2B software homepage, with roughly 2,500 sessions on each side. Changing the primary call to action from “Request a Demo” to “See it in Action” moved conversion from 6.34% to 9.22%. That is a 45% relative lift at 99.21% confidence.

A second test on the same site between 6 and 23 April 2026 changed homepage messaging and replaced rotating cards with static solution links. Top navigation call to action clicks went from 0.9% to 2.2%. Hero call to action clicks went from 1.4% to 3.1%. The share of visitors scrolling past the third section went from 33% to 50%.

Two tests from the same programme that did not work are worth more to you than the two that did.

A demo page layout test in March 2026 produced a 20% relative improvement in conversion at a confidence level below 1%. We logged it as inconclusive and did not ship it.

A header test in January 2026 measured generic click engagement instead of demo form submissions, which produced no usable signal at all. The lesson we recorded: set the goal to the business action, never to engagement.

What should a B2B website call to action say?

Say what happens next, and ask for one thing per section. “See it in Action” outperformed “Request a Demo” in the test above because it describes what the visitor gets rather than what the visitor owes.

One primary action per band of the page is the rule we build to. A row of three equal-weight buttons splits attention and reliably underperforms a single button with one quiet secondary link beside it.

Match the commitment level to the page. A pricing page can ask for a call. A blog post cannot, and asking anyway is how a good article turns into a bounce.

Frequently asked questions

What makes a good B2B website?

A good B2B website answers a buyer’s questions without a sales call and proves its claims. In practice that means four things: clear pricing or a clear reason for withholding it, named client references with permission on file, numbers carrying units and dates, and one obvious next step per page.

How much does a B2B website cost?

Cost tracks the number of page templates and the amount of content, more than the visual design. A small B2B website with five to eight templates and no content migration sits in a different bracket to a redesign that moves several hundred pages. Any agency quoting before it counts your templates and your URLs is guessing.

How long does a B2B website redesign typically take?

Most of the elapsed time goes on content and approvals rather than build. The build itself is usually the shortest phase. Projects slip when nobody owns writing the pages or signing them off.

How do I improve my B2B website conversion rate?

Start with the call to action copy and the number of competing actions per section. Both are cheap to change and quick to test. Redesign the page only once you have clean measurement in place, and set the test goal to the form submission rather than to clicks or engagement.

Search and cost-per-click figures are Semrush, us database, August 2026. A/B test results are our own, measured on client sites and reported without naming them. Third-party research is linked at the point of use.
